guided.title: Explain the DAG file
guided.prompt: Using the Airflow DAG file in the lesson, explain in your own words what `extract >> transform >> load` declares, what the scheduler does with the file, and which line would be a mistake if it called an external API at the top level.
guided.starter:
The >> line:
The scheduler:
A mistake:
guided.solution: `extract >> transform >> load` declares dependencies: transform may start only after extract has succeeded, and load only after transform. The scheduler parses the file repeatedly to learn the DAG, creates DAG runs when their time has come and queues the task instances whose upstream tasks have succeeded; workers run the tasks and every state is written to the metadata database. A call to an external API at the top level of the file (outside a task function) would run on every parse, not once per run, so it would hit the API and slow the scheduler constantly; the call belongs inside a task.
rubric: States that >> orders tasks (upstream before downstream).
Says the scheduler parses the file repeatedly and starts ready task instances.
Identifies top-level code as running on every parse.
Says the call should move into a task.
hints: Think about how often the scheduler reads the file.
Where does work belong in a DAG file?

independent.title: Blast radius of a failure
independent.prompt: Write `downstream(dag, task_id)` returning the sorted list of all tasks that depend on `task_id` directly or indirectly (not including itself). Build the DAG in `BUILD` below and print `downstream(dag, "transform")`, `downstream(dag, "load")` and `downstream(dag, "report")`, one list per line.

independent.title: Rerun only what did not succeed
independent.prompt: Write `run(dag, states, broken)`: go through `dag.order()`; skip tasks already `success` in `states`; a task whose upstream tasks are not all `success` gets `upstream_failed`; a task whose id is in `broken` gets `failed`; otherwise it gets `success`. It updates `states` in place. Run it once with `broken = {"transform"}` on an empty `states` dict and print `sorted(states.items())`, then run it again with `broken = set()` on the same dict and print `sorted(states.items())` again.

independent.title: Design a DAG
independent.prompt: Design the DAG for this job: download a daily file, validate it, load it into a staging table, then in parallel refresh two reporting tables, and finally send a notification. List the tasks, write the dependency line with `>>` (use a list for the parallel tasks), and explain which tasks end up `upstream_failed` if validation fails.
independent.solution: Tasks: `download`, `validate`, `load_staging`, `refresh_sales`, `refresh_customers`, `notify`. Dependencies: `download >> validate >> load_staging >> [refresh_sales, refresh_customers] >> notify`. The two refresh tasks depend only on `load_staging`, so they can run in parallel; `notify` waits for both. If `validate` fails, it is `failed`, and every task after it (`load_staging`, `refresh_sales`, `refresh_customers`, `notify`) is `upstream_failed`; `download` stays `success`. After the cause is fixed, clearing `validate` lets the downstream tasks run again.
rubric: Lists the tasks with unique ids and the right dependency chain.
Shows the two refresh tasks as parallel after load_staging.
Names all four downstream tasks as upstream_failed.
Distinguishes the failed task from the upstream_failed tasks.

environment.note: Airflow is not installed in the browser or in this course environment, so the DAG file in the lesson is shown in a fence, is not executed, and every number or result in the lesson comes from the pure-Python DAG model. To run real Airflow, create a virtual environment and install apache-airflow with the official constraints file for your Airflow and Python versions (pip install "apache-airflow==<version>" --constraint <constraints-url>), then run airflow standalone and put the DAG file in the dags folder; or use the official Docker Compose file from the Airflow documentation. Import paths differ between Airflow 2 and 3, so follow the documentation of the version you install.

checks.question: What does 'acyclic' mean for a DAG?
options: Tasks must run on a fixed time
Following the dependency arrows never leads back to the starting task
Every task has exactly one upstream task
checks.explanation: A cycle would make tasks wait for each other forever. Parallel tasks and tasks with several upstreams are normal.

checks.question: In the model, load and validate both depend only on transform. What does that allow?
options: They must run in alphabetical order
They are in the same level and may run in parallel
checks.explanation: Tasks with no dependency between them are ready at the same moment. The model sorts names only to make output stable.

checks.question: Task B depends on A, C depends on B. A fails. What are the states of B and C?
checks.explanation: Only A raised an error. Tasks that cannot run because of an upstream failure get upstream_failed; they were not attempted.

checks.question: What does this print? calls = {'n': 0}; def f(): calls['n'] += 1; [f() for _ in range(3)]; print(calls['n']) (a model of top-level code and parsing)
checks.explanation: Top-level code runs each time the file is parsed, here three times. Only task functions run once per task instance.

checks.question: Where does Airflow keep the states of task instances?
options: In the memory of the scheduler
checks.explanation: All components share the metadata database; that is why a restarted scheduler can continue and why the UI shows states from every worker.
